submission.natural_language_explanation: This pole fires on colloquial, online/spoken-register English: internet-slang and meme vocabulary (derp, snark, facepalm, noob, epic fail, meme, shitpost, lol, ugh, meh, lowkey, cringe, dope), internet-culture names (xkcd, Tumblr, 4chan, Homestuck, Boing Boing, Pastafarian, Rainbow Dash) and conversational fillers and hedges (basically, kinda, pretty much, literally, thing, such, whatever, just), while it is near-silent on formal edited prose and on ordinary standard words of similar meaning (bad, rough, cool, party, event, Facebook, embarrassing), so swapping a slang word for its formal synonym is predicted to switch it off. Its peaks land mid-word on the register-carrying word itself (e.g. 'ark' in snark) with nothing unusual following, and its output weights promote the same register (shit, fuck, badass, -ish, bullshit, derp, Tumblr), so it is a style detector, not a next-token predictor.

Adventure Time, Mission Impossible, The A-Team, Harry Potter and the new Ghostbusters are about to land on LEGO Dimensions.

Images of the new additions were picked up by users on /r/LEGO, the source of which seems to be early listings on the Mexican version of Amazon. This pretty much breaks the street date of a LEGO Dimensions announcement which is supposed to happen today (June 9th).

The game already features characters, locations, items and more from popular franchises such as DC Comics, Back To The Future and Scooby-Doo.

Adventure Time was already slated to be a LEGO Ideas official set, so it’s appearance on the subreddit wasn’t such a shock. Mission Impossible and The A-Team, on the other hand, are a complete surprise here.

That being said, we still really like these new additions and would love to play them… if it wasn’t for the fact that the game, in any iteration, has still not been released in South Africa.

October is finally in full swing, giving us four (count them: FOUR) movies in one week, one of which is the latest in supernatural horror: Sinister. Truth be told, this is a pretty solid horror movie overall, and gives a fresh spin on the idea of “found footage” movies! It’s brought to us by the producer of Paranormal Activity and Insidious, but doesn’t suffer from some of the issues that both of these had.

Paranormal Activity suffered from being regarded as either incredibly boring or weird and somewhat tense until everything comes to a head at the end. Insidious on the other hand, had a very strong and refreshingly scary feel to it that took a major nosedive in the third act. Sinister manages to maintain a consistent tone to its horror that builds over time…you know, like a proper movie should. It never quite reaches the heights of terror that either movie achieved when at their best, but is a strong effort that’s overall enjoyable.

Of all the characters involved, the most intriguing is easily Ellison Oswalt, played by Ethan Hawke. He’s a true crime writer with a desire to write his best book ever, and the desire quickly turns to an obsession, as the last time he achieved fame was a decade ago with his first book. This obsession drives him to not only move to the same town where the grisly deaths of a family occurred, but into their house where they were murdered!

Now it’s obvious that Sinister is a horror movie, but…the first act of the movie could very well be the first act of a crime thriller along the same lines as Red Dragon (a great movie that should be seen if you haven’t already). This provides the audience a good portrayal of the mental and physical toll that the story takes on Ellison, as well as the family dynamics and how his obsessions affect his wife and children.

Although a successfully scary film, there are two issues that were hard for me to ignore. The first is that the actors playing Ellison’s children, Ashley and Trevor, were less than impressive. It’s no surprise for kid actors to not give great performances, but the daughter’s deadpan performance was incredibly distracting. Then again, my disappointment could be from comparing these kids to Pierce Gagnon, the kid from Looper.

The second and most jarring issue is Sinister’s reliance upon loud music and sounds for many of its scares, like Insidious. Or as my friend the Film Phage put it: “LOUD NOISES!” Despite the annoyingly influential LOUD NOISES…*ahem*…despite the annoyingly influential loud noises and music however, these elements are used in a way that lead to an effectively creepy and unnerving movie. Sure it’s a manipulative tool, but a tool that is used really well.

According to an infrastructure assessment published last quarter, approximately one third of the distribution mains in the metropolitan area have exceeded their design life, and leakage in the oldest districts now accounts for more than fifteen percent of treated volume. The assessment recommends a phased replacement programme, prioritising cast-iron mains installed before 1955, where the incidence of structural defects is highest.

Funding remains the principal obstacle. The utility's capital budget is constrained by a statutory ceiling on bonded debt, and the rate structure has not been revised in more than a decade. Officials have proposed a modest increase in the volumetric tariff, together with a fixed charge intended to stabilise revenue during dry periods. Public consultation on the proposal is expected to begin in the autumn, and the regulator will review the business plan before any increase takes effect.

Water quality monitoring has meanwhile been extended to the tributary intakes upstream of the treatment works. Sampling results from the past two years indicate that nitrate concentrations remain within permitted limits, although seasonal peaks in agricultural runoff occasionally approach the threshold. The utility has therefore commissioned a feasibility study on denitrification at the northern plant. Preliminary estimates suggest capital costs in the range of forty to sixty million, with operating costs dependent on the price of the carbon source.

The assessment also notes that demand management has produced measurable results. Household consumption per capita has declined by approximately nine percent since metering became universal, and the number of reported leaks has fallen following the introduction of acoustic surveys. The authors caution that these gains are partly attributable to a run of mild summers and should not be assumed to persist. They recommend that the conservation programme be maintained and that the replacement schedule be reviewed annually against observed defect data, so that resources are directed to the segments where the risk of service interruption is greatest.

Regulators are expected to publish draft guidance on asset management later this year. Utilities that cannot demonstrate adequate progress may face additional reporting requirements, although no penalties have been proposed at this stage.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
I finally got around to rebuilding the shed shelving last weekend, and the whole project turned into a saga. The plan was simple enough: pull down the old particleboard, measure twice, cut once, screw everything back together. In practice I spent about forty minutes hunting for the stud finder, which turned out to be exactly where I had left it, which is to say on top of the fridge, because of course it was.

The first trip to the hardware store was fine. The second trip, two hours later, was less fine, mostly because I had written the dimensions on the back of a receipt and then left the receipt in the car. The guy at the counter was patient in the way that people are patient when they have seen this exact disaster before, and he walked me through the difference between the two grades of plywood without once making me feel like an idiot, which honestly was a public service.

By Saturday afternoon I had most of the frame up and only two of the cuts were noticeably crooked. I told myself that nobody looks at the underside of a shelf, and that anyone who does look at the underside of a shelf has bigger problems than my carpentry. This is the kind of reasoning that gets a person through a project.

Sunday was priming and painting, which is the part everyone warns you about and which is, in fact, exactly as tedious as advertised. The roller kept shedding fibres into the paint, so the finish has a fuzzy texture that I am choosing to describe as rustic. The neighbour wandered over around four and offered advice that was mostly about how he would have done it, which is a genre of advice I have learned to accept with a nod and a fixed smile.

Still, the shelves are up, they hold the paint cans, and they are level enough that a marble does not roll off. My partner took one look and said it looked great, which I am fairly sure was a kindness rather than an assessment.

On Monday I found the receipt in the car, of course. Total facepalm. Anyway, if anyone needs me I will be in the garage, pretending that the crooked bit was a design choice and scrolling through derp memes until the shame fades. Ten out of ten would build again, which is a total shitpost and you all know it. Meh. At least it holds the paint.
